entities.name: Cao Huan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cao Huan (born 246 CE as Cao Xian, later renamed Cao Huan; died 303 CE) was the fifth and final emperor of the Cao Wei state, reigning from 260 to 265 CE, during China's tumultuous Three Kingdoms period. Though holding the imperial title, Cao Huan functioned primarily as a puppet ruler, his reign entirely dominated by the powerful Sima clan, particularly by Sima Zhao and his son Sima Yan. His historical significance lies not in his personal agency, but in his pivotal, albeit unwilling, role in the transfer of the Mandate of Heaven from the Cao Wei to the nascent Jin Dynasty, marking the end of one of the Three Kingdoms and the prelude to China's eventual reunification under the Jin.

Elevated to the throne at the age of 14 following the deposition of Cao Mao, Cao Huan's rule was characterized by the systematic consolidation of Sima power. Major political and military decisions were made by Sima Zhao, who held the title of regent and later King of Jin. The most significant event of Cao Huan's reign was the conquest of the rival Shu Han state in 263 CE, a military triumph orchestrated by Sima Zhao's generals, which significantly bolstered the Sima clan's prestige and resources, further eroding Cao Wei's nominal authority. Cao Huan himself was a passive observer to these power shifts, his decrees and appointments dictated by the Sima regency.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cao Huan's reign, though lacking personal agency, was historically significant as it marked the formal end of the Cao Wei dynasty and directly facilitated the establishment of the Jin Dynasty, which would eventually reunify China. His forced abdication set a critical precedent for future dynastic changes in Chinese political culture.
